persons.note: THE 1835 POLL LIST ALONE. Read from poll_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G2a), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll_1835 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1835 and nothing says when they came. THE BOUND FALLS AFTER THE SCENE DATE and the record says so rather than narrowing it: the earliest source that names this person is later than 1 July 1835, so they may have arrived after the day this scene models. present_on_scene_date is `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of 1835 — “Bread, A.O.T.” (poll_1835_009, line 294). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Bread' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

merge_ruling.for_merge: THREE INITIALS AGREEING IN ORDER IS AS DISTINCTIVE AS A FORENAME GETS. 'A. O. T.' is not J. or W. H.; the corpus holds no second bearer of those three initials under any surname. A. O. T. Breed is a documented man of the county: the Democrat prints a writ 'dated the 20th day of [March, A.] D. 1834, at the suit of A. O. T. Bre[ed, of the said] county of Cook, and State of Illinois' against an estate in the Territory of Michigan for $1,014; it prints 'Cook Circuit Court, May Term, 1834. Bristol, Howard & Wadham[s] vs. A. O. T. Breed'; the letter list of 1 January 1834 carries him; the Second Presbyterian roll carries the surname. A man suing and sued in the county's own court in 1834 is a man who could be expected on the town's poll of 1835, and the only entry on that poll that could be him is 'Bread, A.O.T.'
merge_ruling.against_merge: NO TITLE REACHED SETS BOTH SPELLINGS, AND ONE OF THEM IS SET EXACTLY ONCE IN THE WHOLE CORPUS. Searched word-boundary over every deposited text and every extracted claim: 'Bread' occurs as a SURNAME in exactly one place — the 1835 poll list, 'Bread, A.O.T.' (voter_lists_1833_1835.txt lines 289 and 294, the transcription printing the page twice) — and every other hit in the corpus is the common noun, including Moses & Kirkland's index entry 'Bread, limitation of, price'. 'Breed' is set by the Democrat, by the Second Presbyterian roll ('Breed, Mrs. Amanda'), by genealogytrails' cemetery history and by Moses & Kirkland — and never beside 'Bread'. The two bodies of evidence do not touch: the town's own roll knows only Bread, and the press, the church and the books know only Breed. Folding on what is left — one letter — is what T-1001 measured and refused. D7, and the cards stay two. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT IS NOT A PAGE BUT A COUNT, in C12's shape moved from the forename to the surname — the closed roll leaves the documented man exactly one entry he can be, and the exhaustion is worked over the whole roll and printed rather than asserted. C12 as written reaches a FORENAME only, so firing it on a surname is itself a rule to write. T-1135 owns that question for Pruyne/Pryne and the rule it writes is the one this pair waits on.
